faq.answer: A production RAG system typically costs $15,000–$30,000 depending on document volume, access-control complexity, and evaluation rigor. The main cost drivers are ingestion pipeline complexity (PDFs, scanned docs, and messy formats cost more than clean markdown) and how strict your accuracy requirements are. We give fixed, scoped estimates after a short discovery.
faq.question: How much does RAG development cost?

faq.answer: RAG connects the model to your documents at query time; fine-tuning bakes knowledge into the model weights during training. RAG is cheaper, faster to update (just re-index the document), and every answer can cite its source. Fine-tuning suits style and behavior changes, not facts. For 'answer from our knowledge base' use cases, RAG wins on cost, freshness, and auditability.
faq.question: What is the difference between RAG and fine-tuning?

faq.answer: Four layers: a chunking strategy matched to your document structure so retrieval finds the right passages; hybrid retrieval (vector + keyword) instead of naive similarity search; a groundedness check that flags answers not supported by retrieved sources; and an evaluation harness of real user questions run on every pipeline change.
faq.question: How do you keep RAG answers accurate?

faq.answer: Yes — this is non-negotiable for enterprise use. We implement permission-aware retrieval: the system filters the vector index by the requesting user's access rights before generation, so confidential documents never leak into answers for unauthorized users. This is designed into the architecture, not bolted on.
faq.question: Can RAG respect our document permissions?

faq.answer: A pilot RAG over a clean document set ships in 3–5 weeks. Complex deployments with messy formats, strict permissions, and evaluation requirements take 8–12 weeks. We start with your highest-value document collection so you see real answers early.
faq.question: How long does it take to build a RAG system?

faq.answer: We work with Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini models plus AWS Bedrock for private deployments, and Pinecone, pgvector, and OpenSearch for vector storage. The choice depends on your data residency, scale, and existing cloud commitments — we recommend the stack, we don't push a favorite.
